We have a new paper out: [*PIONEER: Bayesian Joint Modelling of Mechanistic
Tumour Growth and Time-to-Event Endpoints for Dynamic Prediction of Ongoing
Oncology Trials*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17908). This post is the
plain-language version. It covers what the model is, what we ran it on, and
what it did.

## The interim decision

Around the middle of a Phase 2 oncology trial, a team has to decide whether to
keep going. The difficulty is structural. The decision rests on
progression-free survival and overall survival. Both endpoints measure how long
patients go without progressing or dying, so at an interim look most patients'
outcomes are still unfolding. A patient with nothing recorded yet is not known
to be doing well. We have not followed them long enough to say. Any median is a
long way off, and the primary endpoint may not read out for another year or
more.

Waiting has a cost, and so does guessing. Teams use what is available: a
p-value on immature data, a comparison against a historical control, or an
assumed effect size and a conditional-power calculation. None of these fully
answers the actual question, which is what the trial will look like when it
finishes.

## The evidence already in hand

This observation motivated the paper. At every interim cut-off, the trial holds
a dense, information-rich record that a survival analysis almost entirely
discards.

Patients are scanned on a schedule. Each scan yields a sum of longest
diameters, a number for how much tumour is present. Over months, each patient
accumulates a trajectory. A conventional interim analysis compresses that
trajectory into a single fact: "progressed at week 14" or "not yet progressed".
Six measurements tracing a tumour shrinking, bottoming out, and starting to
regrow become one event indicator and one date.

The shape of the trajectory indicates where a patient is heading. Consider a
tumour still shrinking at last contact and one that bottomed out three months
ago and has been climbing since. These two patients are in very different
positions. A survival model that sees only "no event yet" treats them
identically.

## The model, in three pieces

The framework couples three components and fits them simultaneously, under a
single posterior. The simultaneous fit is the central design choice.

**Tumour dynamics.** A mechanistic state-space submodel infers each patient's
latent tumour trajectory from their sparse, noisy scan measurements. It is a
two-component decomposition: tumour burden is split into a *treatment-responsive*
compartment that shrinks under therapy and a *refractory* compartment that does
not. Growth is Gompertz-attenuated, so regrowth slows as burden accumulates
instead of growing exponentially. The familiar shrink-then-regrow curve is not
imposed. It emerges when the two compartments cross over.

**Clinical events.** A multistate proportional-hazard submodel handles the
events that happen to patients: progression, death with and without prior
progression, and dropout. It treats them as transitions between states, not as
a single lumped endpoint. The latent tumour trajectories enter this submodel as
*time-varying covariates*. The hazard therefore responds to where a patient's
tumour is going, in addition to their baseline risk factors.

**One joint fit.** Information flows in both directions. Latent trajectories
drive the hazards, and the event data simultaneously sharpen the tumour
dynamics through the shared likelihood. A patient who progresses tells the
model something about their tumour trajectory.

This two-way flow distinguishes the approach from the standard two-stage
pharmacometric workflow. In that workflow you fit tumour kinetics first,
extract summary statistics (growth rate, time to nadir, week-8 burden), and
plug them into a survival model as though they were measured without error.
Two-stage inheritance discards the uncertainty in stage one and attenuates the
association in stage two. Fitting jointly avoids both problems. The cost is a
considerably harder posterior.

Every endpoint (PFS, OS, objective response rate) is then derived from that
single joint posterior in one forward simulation pass. There are no separate
models to reconcile after the fact. One model is simulated forward, with full
parameter uncertainty carried through.

## The data

The case study is first-line extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. It uses
two completed trials obtained through [Project Data
Sphere](https://www.projectdatasphere.org/), which makes de-identified trial
data available to registered researchers, so the analysis can be checked
independently.

| | Trial | Role | N |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Target** | Lilly CXCR4 (I2V-MC-CXAC) | the trial being forecast | 78 |
| **Historical** | Amgen 20010145 (darbepoetin alfa) | the trial borrowed from | 419 |

The design is a *retrospective replay*. Both trials are finished, so we know the
answer. The model is re-fit at successive historical cut-offs, given only the
data that existed at that moment, and its forecast is compared against the
mature result it had not yet seen. This is leave-future-out cross-validation.
Adapting it to this setting is fiddly, so I wrote [a separate post about
it](lfo-beyond-time-series.qmd).

::: {.wide-figure}
```{julia}
#| label: fig-sld
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Observed tumour burden over time, both trials. The line is the median sum of longest diameters across patients in each six-week window; the band spans the middle half of patients. Windows with fewer than ten patients are not shown. Both trials show the same steep early decline and flattening. Later regrowth is less visible here than in individual patients, because patients who progress stop contributing scans. The shared shape is the empirical basis for pooling growth kinetics across the trials."
#| fig-height: 4.2
# A cross-patient summary rather than one line per patient: the Project Data
# Sphere terms allow publishing only the data reasonably necessary to report
# the results (see _julia/site_figures.jl).
fig_sld_summary(color = SiteTheme.INK, band_color = (SiteTheme.OBS_TEAL, 0.3))
```
:::

Nine patients cannot determine a survival curve on their own. The 419
historical patients fill that gap. Growth kinetics are partially pooled across
both trials. The degree of borrowing is learned from the data, not fixed in
advance. The target trial's own patients still decide the final answer. The
historical trial supplies the shape of the process.

## Results

The first result is one level below the survival curves. The mechanistic
submodel produces a trajectory for each patient and continues it past the
patient's last measurement.

::: {.wide-figure}
```{julia}
#| label: fig-sld-censored
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Model-inferred tumour burden for twelve patients still progression-free at their last scan, three from each arm of the two trials (rows). Teal is the model's fit over the observed phase, up to each patient's last measurement; terracotta is its forecast beyond it, fading out where the model expects progression. Bands are 50% and 80% credible intervals. The raw scan values and axis scales are omitted under the data-use terms; each panel runs from zero at the start of treatment."
#| fig-height: 5.5
fig_sld_censored_site(obs_color = SiteTheme.OBS_TEAL,
                      obs_colormap = SiteTheme.OBS_BAND,
                      forecast_color = SiteTheme.ACCENT_SOFT,
                      forecast_colormap = SiteTheme.FORECAST_BAND)
```
:::

The survival forecasts depend on this step. Each of these patients is censored
(no progression recorded), so a conventional analysis says nothing about them
beyond "still enrolled". The model carries each one forward with an explicit
uncertainty band. Those simulated trajectories drive the hazard, and the hazard
produces the survival curve below.

The next figure shows the retrospective replay for progression-free survival.
Each column is a cut-off, labelled with how many target-trial patients had
enrolled by then.

::: {.wide-figure}
```{julia}
#| label: fig-lfo-pfs
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Progression-free survival by treatment arm (rows). Columns are successive cut-offs (months 4, 11 and 19), each labelled with the target-trial patients observed by then. The fourth column is the same estimand fit to complete data, where observed and mature curves necessarily coincide."
#| fig-height: 5.5
fig_lfo_pfs()
```
:::

At month 4, with nine patients enrolled, the 80% credible band already covers
the mature Kaplan-Meier curve. That curve is the dashed line. The model had not
seen it and would not see it for another fifteen months. The band is also very
wide. That width is correct for what nine patients can support.

By month 11, at 39 patients, the forecast has tightened onto the mature
curve. Tracking the median directly makes the convergence easier to read:

:::: {.wide-figure}

::: {layout-ncol=2}

```{julia}
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 6.0
fig_median_pfs(show_legend = false)
```

```{julia}

fig_median_os(show_category_labels = false, show_legend = false)
```

```{julia}
fig_cutoff_legend()
```

::::

Overall survival converges at month 11, at least eight months before it read
out. The forecast includes quantified uncertainty. The OS intervals are wider
than the PFS intervals throughout. This is expected. OS routes through
progression, direct death, and dropout, and the forecast carries all three.

## What this does and does not show

Coverage is not the same thing as a decision. The month-4 band contains the
truth, which says the model was not wrong. It does not say the model was useful
at month 4. A band that wide is consistent with several conclusions at once. A
decision needs an interval narrow enough to separate "keep going" from "stop",
and at month 4 this one is not. Read properly, the month-4 result says to wait.

This behaviour is a property of the model, not an accident. When the model
cannot forecast well, the output shows it. Uncertainty about the tumour
parameters, the hazards, and where each unfinished trajectory is heading is
carried through the same posterior into the endpoint. Sparse or uninformative
data therefore produce a wide band. The month-4 panel is the model reporting
that nine patients do not determine a survival curve. There is no separate
diagnostic to consult. There is also no failure mode in which a
confident-looking number comes out of data that cannot support it. The width of
the band is the diagnostic, and it appears in the same picture as the
answer.^[This has one important limit. Wide intervals reflect the uncertainty
the model can see: parameter uncertainty and predictive variability given its
structure. They do not reflect the possibility that the structure itself is
wrong. A misspecified mechanism can be confidently mistaken, producing narrow
bands around the wrong curve, and nothing internal to the posterior will show
it. For that reason the retrospective replay above is important. It is an
external check, on data the model had not seen, that the intervals mean what
they claim.]

The value of the approach is knowing, at every cut-off, which conclusions the
data currently support and which they do not. The model reports this on the
endpoint's own scale, in months of survival, instead of as a single probability
of success.

The usual interim tools differ from each other on this point. *Conditional
power* gives the chance of a significant result at the final analysis given an
assumed treatment effect. That assumption then becomes the subject of debate,
because the answer moves with it. *Bayesian predictive probability of success*
improves on this. It integrates over the posterior for the effect instead of
fixing it. Both methods, however, reduce the picture to one number relative to
a pre-specified success threshold. Forecasting the mature curve keeps the
estimate and the threshold separate. The model says where the endpoint is
heading and how uncertain that is. The position of the go/no-go line remains an
explicit statement of risk tolerance. That choice belongs to the stakeholder,
not the model.

The main limitation is scope: one indication, two trials, one retrospective
replay. This is evidence that the approach works. It is not evidence about how
well it works in general. Extensive-stage SCLC is a fast-moving disease with a
strong tumour-burden signal, which makes it a comparatively favourable setting.

The next question is whether the approach holds up elsewhere. A second
application, in a different disease with a different set of trials, is in
progress. Results will follow in a later post.

## Where to go next

The [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17908) has the full specification: the
state-space formulation, the multistate hazard structure, the hierarchical
priors, and the cross-validation methodology. For the cross-validation piece on
its own, [the LFO post](lfo-beyond-time-series.qmd) works through what breaks
when you take a method built for univariate time series into a setting with
staggered enrolment and two different observation clocks.

I would be glad to hear from anyone working on something structurally similar:
a latent mechanistic process generating both a longitudinal measurement stream
and an event stream, with actors entering at different times. The same
skeleton applies outside oncology.
